subject: biology

questions.content: Which of these is a microorganism that has no nucleus and is classed as a prokaryote?
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes: their DNA floats freely in the cytoplasm because they have no nucleus. Amoeba, yeast and algae are eukaryotes.

questions.content: Which type of microorganism is made of genetic material inside a protein coat and can only reproduce inside a host cell?
questions.explanation: Viruses are not cells. They have genetic material inside a protein coat and must take over a host cell to make copies of themselves.

questions.content: Yeast is a single-celled microorganism. To which group does it belong?
questions.explanation: Yeast is a single-celled fungus. It has a nucleus and a cell wall, and it reproduces by budding.

questions.content: Bacteria multiply by splitting in two. What is this process called?
questions.explanation: Binary fission is asexual reproduction in which one bacterial cell copies its DNA and then divides into two identical cells.

questions.content: Which condition is needed for most bacteria to grow quickly?
questions.explanation: Bacteria grow fastest when it is warm, moist and nutrients are available. Cold, dry or very bright conditions slow or stop growth.

questions.content: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting with one cell, how many cells will there be after 2 hours if nothing limits growth?
questions.explanation: Two hours is 120 minutes, which is 6 divisions of 20 minutes. Each division doubles the number, so 2 to the power 6 gives 64 cells.

questions.content: Which feature do bacteria and fungi both have that animal cells do not?
questions.explanation: Bacteria and fungi both have a cell wall (made of different materials). Animal cells have only a cell membrane.

questions.content: Why can a virus not be grown on nutrient agar the way bacteria can?
options: Viruses are too large to fit on agar
Viruses need living host cells to reproduce
Viruses do not contain genetic material
questions.explanation: Viruses have no metabolism of their own, so they can only reproduce inside living host cells. Nutrient agar contains food but no living cells.

questions.content: A student wants to grow bacteria in a lab safely. Which step is part of aseptic technique?
options: Leaving the dish lid off to let air in
Passing the inoculating loop through a flame before use
Incubating the dish at 37 degrees Celsius with the lid taped fully shut
Growing the culture at 60 degrees Celsius
questions.explanation: Flaming the loop sterilises it, so only the intended bacteria are transferred. Aseptic technique aims to stop unwanted microbes entering or escaping the culture.

questions.content: Why are school laboratories told to incubate bacterial cultures at about 25 degrees Celsius rather than 37 degrees Celsius?
options: Bacteria cannot grow at 37 degrees Celsius
25 degrees Celsius is better for human pathogens
The lower temperature makes harmful human pathogens less likely to grow
questions.explanation: Human pathogens grow best near body temperature, 37 degrees Celsius. Using a lower temperature favours harmless environmental bacteria and reduces risk.

questions.content: A graph of bacterial numbers over time shows a lag phase, then a steep rise. What is happening in the steep rise?
options: Cells are dying faster than they divide
Cells are dividing at a steady, rapid rate
Cells are adjusting to the new nutrients
questions.explanation: The steep rise is the exponential (log) phase, when conditions are good and cells divide at a constant rapid rate. The lag phase is when they adjust first.

questions.content: Which of these is a protist?
questions.explanation: Amoeba is a single-celled eukaryote that is not a plant, animal or fungus, so it is a protist. Penicillium is a fungus, E. coli is a bacterium and influenza is a virus.

questions.content: Which statement about bacterial DNA is correct?
options: It is enclosed in a nuclear membrane
It forms a single loop in the cytoplasm, often with small extra rings called plasmids
It is found only in the cell wall
questions.explanation: Bacteria have one circular chromosome in the cytoplasm and often carry plasmids, small rings of DNA that can carry extra genes such as antibiotic resistance.

questions.content: A culture has 1,000 bacteria at time zero and 8,000 bacteria 90 minutes later. What is the doubling time, assuming exponential growth?
questions.explanation: 8,000 is 1,000 doubled 3 times (1,000 to 2,000 to 4,000 to 8,000). Three doublings in 90 minutes means one doubling every 30 minutes.

questions.content: In a closed flask with limited food, bacterial growth levels off. Which explanation is best?
options: Bacteria stop dividing because they become too large
Nutrients are used up and waste products build up, so deaths balance new cells
questions.explanation: In a closed system, nutrients run out and toxic waste accumulates. The stationary phase is reached when the rate of cell death equals the rate of division.

questions.content: A clear zone appears around a disc of antiseptic on a lawn of bacteria. A larger clear zone means that the antiseptic is...
questions.explanation: The clear zone shows where bacteria could not grow. The bigger the zone, the further the antiseptic diffused while still preventing growth, so the more effective it is.

questions.content: Which feature allows spore-forming bacteria to survive boiling water better than ordinary bacterial cells?
options: They form a tough dormant structure around their DNA
questions.explanation: Some bacteria form endospores, thick-walled dormant structures that resist heat, drying and chemicals. This is why food and equipment may need pressure heating to be sterilised.

questions.content: A mutation lets one bacterium survive an antibiotic. After several generations in the presence of the antibiotic, most of the population is resistant. Which process explains this?
options: The antibiotic causes all bacteria to mutate in the same way
Natural selection: resistant bacteria survive and reproduce
The bacteria choose to become resistant
The antibiotic turns into food for bacteria
questions.explanation: Resistance arises by random mutation. The antibiotic kills non-resistant cells, so the resistant ones reproduce and pass on the gene, which is natural selection.

note:
Microorganisms are living things too small to see without a microscope. The main groups are bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists, and they differ greatly in structure.

Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes. A prokaryote has no nucleus. Its DNA is a single circular chromosome lying free in the cytoplasm, and many bacteria also carry small rings of extra DNA called plasmids. Bacteria have a cell wall, a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes. Some have a tail-like flagellum to swim. They come in three common shapes: spheres (cocci), rods (bacilli) and spirals.

Viruses are much smaller than bacteria and are not made of cells. A virus is a piece of genetic material, DNA or RNA, inside a protein coat. It has no cytoplasm and no metabolism, so it cannot feed, grow or reproduce on its own. To make more viruses it must enter a host cell and use the cell's own machinery. Because of this, many biologists describe viruses as being on the border of living and non-living.

Fungi can be single-celled, like yeast, or made of thread-like hyphae, like moulds and mushrooms. Fungal cells are eukaryotic: they have a nucleus, and they also have a cell wall. They feed by releasing enzymes onto food and absorbing the digested products. Protists are a mixed group of single-celled eukaryotes, such as Amoeba and Paramecium, that are not plants, animals or fungi.

Bacteria reproduce by binary fission. The cell copies its DNA, grows, and then splits into two identical daughter cells. Under ideal conditions some bacteria can divide every 20 minutes. This means a population doubles each cycle, which is exponential growth. After n divisions, one cell becomes 2 to the power n cells. After 10 divisions that is 1,024 cells, and after 20 divisions it is more than a million.

The growth of a bacterial population in a closed container follows four phases. In the lag phase, cells adjust to their new surroundings and numbers barely change. In the exponential or log phase, conditions are ideal and numbers climb steeply. In the stationary phase, food begins to run out and waste builds up, so the number of new cells equals the number of cells dying. In the death phase, deaths outnumber divisions and the population falls.

Growth depends on temperature, moisture, nutrients, oxygen and pH. Most bacteria that infect humans grow best near 37 degrees Celsius, body temperature. Cold slows growth, which is why we refrigerate food, and heat above about 60 degrees Celsius kills most bacteria, which is why we cook it. Some bacteria produce spores, tough dormant structures that survive heat and drying until conditions improve.

In the laboratory, microbes are grown on nutrient agar in Petri dishes. Aseptic technique prevents contamination: equipment is sterilised, an inoculating loop is flamed, the lid is only briefly lifted, and the dish is taped but not sealed completely. In school laboratories cultures are usually incubated at about 25 degrees Celsius to avoid growing human pathogens.

To test antibiotics or antiseptics, discs soaked in each substance are placed on a lawn of bacteria. After incubation, a clear zone shows where bacteria could not grow. A larger clear zone means a more effective substance. The area of the zone can be calculated using the formula for the area of a circle, pi multiplied by the radius squared.

Exam tip: always link a bacterial number to the number of doublings. Work out how many divisions fit into the time, then apply 2 to the power n.

flashcards.back: A cell with no nucleus; its DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm. Bacteria are prokaryotes.
Asexual reproduction in bacteria: one cell copies its DNA and splits into two identical cells.
A small extra ring of DNA in bacteria that can carry genes such as antibiotic resistance.

flashcards.front: Why is a virus not a cell?
flashcards.back: It is only genetic material in a protein coat, with no cytoplasm or metabolism, so it can only reproduce inside a host cell.
Lag, exponential (log), stationary, death.

flashcards.front: Number of bacteria after n doublings from one cell
flashcards.back: 2 to the power n.
Methods that stop unwanted microbes contaminating a culture, such as flaming the loop and lifting the lid only briefly.

flashcards.front: Why incubate school cultures at about 25 degrees Celsius?
flashcards.back: Human pathogens grow best near 37 degrees Celsius, so the cooler temperature makes them less likely to grow.

flashcards.front: Clear zone on an agar plate
flashcards.back: An area around a disc where bacteria could not grow; a bigger zone means a more effective antibiotic or antiseptic.

subject: biology

questions.content: Which organisms break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil?
questions.explanation: Decomposers, mainly bacteria and fungi, feed on dead organic matter and release nutrients back into the soil.

questions.content: Which two groups are the main decomposers?
questions.explanation: Bacteria and fungi are the main decomposers. They release enzymes that digest dead material.

questions.content: Which of these conditions speeds up decomposition?
questions.explanation: Warm, moist conditions with oxygen let decomposers grow and work quickly. Cold or dry conditions slow them down.

questions.content: What is compost?
options: Decomposed plant and food waste used to improve soil
questions.explanation: Compost is dead plant and food material broken down by decomposers into a nutrient-rich material that improves soil.

questions.content: What do decomposers release into the air when they respire?
questions.explanation: Decomposers respire, so they release carbon dioxide, which returns carbon to the atmosphere for plants to use in photosynthesis.

questions.content: Why do decomposers release enzymes onto dead material outside their bodies?
options: To digest large molecules into small ones they can absorb
questions.explanation: Decomposers do external digestion. Enzymes break large molecules such as proteins and carbohydrates into small soluble ones that can be absorbed.

questions.content: Food in a fridge stays fresh longer than food left on a warm bench. What is the best explanation?
options: Low temperature slows enzyme activity and microbial growth
questions.explanation: Cold does not kill most microbes, but it slows their enzymes and metabolism, so they grow and decompose food much more slowly.

questions.content: A farmer adds compost to a field. How does this help crop growth?
options: It adds mineral nutrients and improves soil structure
It removes all water from the soil
It kills all the soil organisms
questions.explanation: Compost releases mineral ions such as nitrates and phosphates as it decomposes and improves soil structure, helping water retention and root growth.

questions.content: Which process puts carbon from dead organisms back into the atmosphere?
questions.explanation: When decomposers feed on dead matter they respire, releasing carbon dioxide into the air. This returns carbon to the atmosphere.

questions.content: Which organisms convert ammonia from decaying matter into nitrites and nitrates?
questions.explanation: Nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonia to nitrites and then to nitrates, which plants can absorb through their roots.

questions.content: Waterlogged soil has very little oxygen. Which change would you expect there?
questions.explanation: Aerobic decomposers need oxygen for respiration. In waterlogged soil they are limited, so decomposition slows, and denitrifying bacteria can remove nitrate.

questions.content: In a compost heap, the centre becomes warmer than the outside. Why?
questions.explanation: Respiration by billions of decomposers releases energy as heat, so the middle of a large compost heap warms up.

questions.content: Dead leaves on a forest floor decay faster in summer than in winter. What is the main reason?
options: There is more oxygen in winter
questions.explanation: Higher temperatures increase the rate of enzyme activity and microbial growth, so decomposition is faster in warm months.

questions.content: A student places equal masses of leaf litter in four bags at different temperatures and measures mass loss after 4 weeks. The 35 degrees Celsius bag lost the most mass. Why must the water content be kept the same in every bag?
options: Moisture is a variable that also affects decomposition, so it must be controlled
questions.explanation: Only temperature should differ. If moisture also varied, any difference in mass loss could not be assigned to temperature alone, so moisture is a control variable.

questions.content: Why does the mass of dry leaf litter fall during decomposition even though the microbes are growing?
options: Microbes convert much of the carbon into carbon dioxide and water by respiration
questions.explanation: Most of the carbon in the litter is lost to the air as carbon dioxide through respiration, and some as water vapour, so the dry mass decreases.

questions.content: Which statement best describes why recycling of nutrients is essential in an ecosystem?
options: Nutrients are used up and cannot be replaced
The supply of mineral ions is limited, so decomposers make them available again for producers
Producers get minerals only from the air
questions.explanation: Atoms are not created. Without decomposers, nutrients would stay locked in dead matter, producers would run out of mineral ions and the food web would collapse.

questions.content: A fungus can break down dead wood while many bacteria cannot. Which adaptation best explains this?
options: It makes thread-like hyphae and enzymes that digest tough cellulose and lignin
questions.explanation: Fungal hyphae penetrate the wood and release enzymes that digest tough materials such as cellulose and lignin that most bacteria cannot digest efficiently.

questions.content: Peat bogs preserve dead plant material for thousands of years. Which combination of conditions best explains this?
options: Warm, dry and rich in oxygen
Waterlogged, acidic and low in oxygen
questions.explanation: Waterlogging limits oxygen and the acidic conditions reduce microbial activity, so decomposition is extremely slow and plant material accumulates as peat.

note:
Decomposition is the breakdown of dead organisms and waste into simpler substances. It is carried out by decomposers, mainly bacteria and fungi, and it is essential because it returns nutrients to the soil and carbon to the air so that producers can use them again.

Decomposers feed in a special way called extracellular or external digestion. They release enzymes onto dead leaves, wood, bodies or waste. The enzymes break large molecules such as proteins, starch and fats into small soluble molecules, which the decomposer then absorbs. The decomposer uses some of these molecules for growth and respires others to release energy. Respiration releases carbon dioxide, which returns carbon to the atmosphere.

The rate of decomposition depends on several factors. Temperature is important because enzymes work faster when it is warm, up to an optimum. Cold slows decomposers down, which is why a fridge keeps food fresh and why dead material decays slowly in cold climates. Moisture is also needed because microbes need water for their enzymes and for growth. Oxygen matters because most decomposers respire aerobically. Where oxygen is missing, as in waterlogged soil or a peat bog, decomposition is very slow, and so plant remains can build up as peat. Acidity can also reduce activity. The type of material matters too: soft tissues decompose quickly, whereas tough woody material containing lignin and cellulose breaks down slowly.

Compost is a human use of decomposition. Gardeners pile up plant waste and vegetable scraps, keep it damp, and turn it to let in oxygen. Decomposers multiply and release heat from respiration, so the middle of the pile warms up, often to 50 degrees Celsius or more. After some weeks the waste has become a dark, crumbly compost that supplies mineral ions and improves soil structure and water retention.

Nutrient cycles depend on decomposers. In the carbon cycle, plants take carbon dioxide from the air in photosynthesis, animals eat plants, and carbon returns to the air by respiration, including that of decomposers. Dead material that is not decomposed, such as under waterlogged conditions, can eventually form fossil fuels. In the nitrogen cycle, decomposers break down proteins and urea into ammonia. Nitrifying bacteria then convert ammonia to nitrites and nitrates, which plants absorb to make proteins. Denitrifying bacteria, found in waterlogged soil, convert nitrates back to nitrogen gas.

Investigating decomposition is a common practical. A student may bury equal masses of leaf litter in bags at different temperatures and measure the mass loss after some weeks. The independent variable is temperature, the dependent variable is mass lost, and control variables include the type and mass of leaf, moisture, the size of the bag and the time. A repeat of each condition improves reliability.

Exam tip: when explaining why decomposition is faster in a given situation, name the factor, name the effect on the enzymes or decomposers, and then link to the faster release of carbon dioxide or nutrients.

flashcards.back: Organisms, mainly bacteria and fungi, that break down dead organisms and waste and return nutrients to the environment.
Decomposers release enzymes onto food outside their body, then absorb the small soluble products.
Warmth, moisture, oxygen and soft or small pieces of material.
Microbes respire and release energy as heat.

flashcards.front: Why is decomposition slow in a peat bog?
flashcards.back: It is waterlogged, acidic and low in oxygen, so decomposer activity is very low.
Convert ammonia into nitrites and then nitrates, which plants can absorb.
Convert nitrates back to nitrogen gas, mainly in waterlogged soil.

flashcards.front: How does decomposition return carbon to the air?
flashcards.back: Decomposers respire and release carbon dioxide.

flashcards.front: Control variables in a leaf decay experiment
flashcards.back: Type and mass of leaf, moisture, bag size and time. Only temperature changes.

subject: biology

questions.content: Which microorganism is used to make bread rise?
questions.explanation: Yeast respires and produces carbon dioxide, which forms bubbles in dough and makes it rise.

questions.content: Which bacteria are used to turn milk into yoghurt?
questions.explanation: Lactobacillus bacteria ferment lactose in milk into lactic acid, which thickens the milk and gives yoghurt its sour taste.

questions.content: Which gas makes bread dough rise?
questions.explanation: Yeast produces carbon dioxide during fermentation. The gas is trapped in the dough, which expands.

questions.content: Yeast is used to make alcoholic drinks. What does yeast turn sugar into during this process?
questions.explanation: In anaerobic respiration, yeast converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide. This is alcoholic fermentation.

questions.content: Which mould is used to produce the antibiotic penicillin?
questions.explanation: Penicillin was discovered from the fungus Penicillium notatum, and it is still produced industrially from related Penicillium moulds.

questions.content: What is the word equation for alcoholic fermentation in yeast?
options: Glucose gives ethanol plus carbon dioxide
Glucose plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide plus water
Carbon dioxide plus water gives glucose
questions.explanation: Yeast respires anaerobically: glucose produces ethanol and carbon dioxide, and releases a small amount of energy.

questions.content: Why is milk heated (pasteurised) before yoghurt is made?
options: To kill unwanted microbes so only the chosen bacteria grow
questions.explanation: Pasteurisation kills harmful and competing microbes, so the starter culture of Lactobacillus can ferment the milk without interference.

questions.content: What is the role of lactic acid in yoghurt making?
options: It lowers the pH and causes milk proteins to clot
questions.explanation: Lactic acid lowers the pH, which makes milk proteins coagulate and thicken the milk. The acidity also helps to preserve the yoghurt.

questions.content: A fermenter is used to grow microbes industrially. Which of these is a reason for having a water jacket around it?
options: To keep the temperature at the optimum
questions.explanation: Microbial respiration releases heat. A water jacket carries heat away so the temperature stays at the optimum for the microbe's enzymes.

questions.content: Why is the contents of an industrial fermenter stirred?
options: To mix nutrients, oxygen and microbes evenly
questions.explanation: Stirring spreads nutrients, oxygen and heat evenly and stops microbes settling, so all cells have good conditions for growth.

questions.content: Mycoprotein is a food made from a fungus. Why is it described as a good protein source?
options: It is fast to grow and is high in protein and low in fat
questions.explanation: The fungus grows quickly in fermenters on cheap sugar and produces protein-rich biomass with little fat, making it a useful alternative protein.

questions.content: Which of these is a benefit of making enzymes using microbes rather than extracting them from animals?
options: Microbes grow quickly and cheaply in large amounts
Microbes make enzymes that never denature
questions.explanation: Microbes reproduce rapidly and can be grown in controlled fermenters on cheap substrates, so large amounts of enzyme are produced economically.

questions.content: Which food-preservation method works mainly by removing water so microbes cannot grow?
questions.explanation: Drying removes the water that microbes need for growth, so food such as dried fruit or pasta lasts a long time.

questions.content: Dough is left for an hour in a warm place and doubles in size. At 5 degrees Celsius it barely changes. Which explanation is best?
options: Yeast enzymes work faster in the warm place so more carbon dioxide is made
Yeast dies instantly at 5 degrees Celsius
The cold makes carbon dioxide dissolve completely
questions.explanation: Respiration in yeast is enzyme-controlled. Higher temperature, up to an optimum, means more frequent collisions and faster gas production. Cold slows the enzymes but does not necessarily kill the yeast.

questions.content: Bakers add a little sugar to dough. What is its purpose?
options: It provides glucose for yeast respiration
questions.explanation: Yeast uses sugars as its substrate. Extra sugar supplies glucose for fermentation, so more carbon dioxide is made and the dough rises faster.

questions.content: A brewing fermenter must be kept free of oxygen during ethanol production. Which reason is correct?
options: With plenty of oxygen yeast would respire aerobically, making carbon dioxide and water instead of ethanol
questions.explanation: Ethanol is made only in anaerobic respiration. With oxygen, yeast respires aerobically to carbon dioxide and water, releasing more energy and producing no ethanol.

questions.content: A fermenter runs a batch process, adding nutrients once and harvesting at the end. A different design adds nutrients and removes product continuously. What is a likely advantage of the continuous design?
options: It produces product constantly and avoids stopping to clean between batches
questions.explanation: Continuous culture keeps microbes in the exponential phase and produces steady output, reducing downtime. It is however harder to keep sterile for long periods.

questions.content: Which statement correctly compares fermentation in yeast and lactic acid fermentation in Lactobacillus?
options: Both are anaerobic, but yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide while Lactobacillus makes lactic acid
Yeast makes lactic acid and Lactobacillus makes ethanol
questions.explanation: Both are forms of anaerobic respiration, but the products differ: yeast forms ethanol and carbon dioxide, and Lactobacillus forms lactic acid and no gas.

note:
Humans have used microorganisms for thousands of years to make food, and today they are also grown on a huge scale in industry. The key idea is that microbes respire and make useful products, and we control the conditions so they work efficiently.

Yeast and fermentation. Yeast is a single-celled fungus. When there is little or no oxygen, it carries out anaerobic respiration, also called alcoholic fermentation. Glucose is converted to ethanol and carbon dioxide, with a small release of energy. In baking, the carbon dioxide forms bubbles that make the dough rise, and the ethanol evaporates in the oven. In brewing and wine making, the ethanol is the desired product. The speed of fermentation depends on temperature, because enzymes work faster when it is warm up to an optimum. Bakers therefore leave dough in a warm place and add a little sugar to give the yeast glucose.

Bacteria in dairy products. Yoghurt and cheese are made using Lactobacillus and related bacteria. Milk is first pasteurised, meaning heated to kill unwanted microbes, and then cooled to about 40 degrees Celsius. A starter culture of bacteria is added. The bacteria ferment the sugar lactose into lactic acid. The acid lowers the pH and makes milk proteins clot and thicken, and it also preserves the product by making conditions too acidic for many spoilage microbes.

Mycoprotein. A fungus is grown in large fermenters on glucose syrup to produce mycoprotein, a protein-rich food sold as a meat alternative. It grows quickly, is high in protein and fibre, and is low in fat.

Penicillin and enzymes. The antibiotic penicillin is made by the mould Penicillium. Industrial enzymes such as the proteases in biological washing powders and the amylases that turn starch into syrup are also made by microbes, because microbes grow quickly and cheaply in large quantities.

Industrial fermenters. A fermenter is a large, sterile vessel in which microbes are grown under controlled conditions. It has a stirrer to mix contents and spread oxygen and nutrients, a water jacket to remove heat released by respiration, probes to monitor temperature and pH, and an air supply for aerobic microbes. Everything is sterilised first so that contaminating microbes cannot compete with the useful ones. In batch culture, a fixed amount of nutrient is added and the product is collected at the end. In continuous culture, nutrients are added and product removed all the time, which gives steady output but is harder to keep sterile.

Preserving food. Microbes can also spoil food, so people have developed preservation methods. Refrigeration and freezing slow microbial growth. Drying and adding salt or sugar remove available water. Pickling in vinegar lowers the pH. Heating, such as canning, kills microbes. Each method works by removing at least one of the conditions microbes need: warmth, water, nutrients or suitable pH.

Exam tip: when asked why a condition is controlled in a fermenter, name the condition, name the effect on enzymes or the microbe, and link it to the yield of product.

flashcards.back: Glucose gives ethanol plus carbon dioxide (anaerobic respiration in yeast).
Yeast produces carbon dioxide, which forms bubbles trapped in the dough.
Pasteurised milk is fermented by Lactobacillus, which turns lactose into lactic acid and thickens the milk.
To kill unwanted microbes so the starter culture can grow.
A protein-rich food made from a fungus grown in fermenters; low in fat and used as a meat alternative.

flashcards.front: Why does a fermenter have a water jacket?
flashcards.back: To remove heat released by microbial respiration and keep the temperature at the optimum.
To mix nutrients, oxygen, heat and microbes evenly.
Batch: fixed nutrients and one harvest. Continuous: nutrients added and product removed all the time.
They remove a condition microbes need: warmth, water, nutrients or suitable pH.
